title: Quorum-Based Replication
explain: Quorum-based replication commits an operation once a majority, or another quorum, of replicas has it, so progress never depends on one node. People mix up two flavours: tunable Dynamo-style quorums, which are leaderless and eventually consistent, and consensus quorums such as Raft, where an elected leader orders a log and commits it on a majority.
model:
```
Tunable (Dynamo)               Consensus (Raft / Paxos)
no leader                      elected leader orders a log
per request W, R: W+R > N      entry committed when a majority stores it
available, "mostly fresh"      one history, strong consistency
repaired in background         minority side stops
```

1. **Tunable quorums:** see [leaderless quorum](#/sd/f/leaderless-quorum).
2. **Consensus quorums:** see [consensus](#/sd/f/consensus) and [Raft](#/sd/f/raft).

**Majority arithmetic:** a cluster of N tolerates floor((N−1)/2) failures: 3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2, 7 tolerates 3. **Even sizes buy nothing**: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority and still tolerate 1, so use odd sizes.

**Why majorities:** any two majorities overlap in at least one node, so two disjoint partitions cannot both make progress. That prevents split brain without needing the dead node to confirm it is dead; the minority side simply stops accepting writes.

**Costs:** each commit waits for the replica that completes the majority, which becomes a cross-region round trip if replicas span regions ([multi-region](#/sd/f/multi-region)). Quorums defend against crashes and partitions, not corrupted or malicious nodes.

details.q: How many failures does a 7-node majority group tolerate?
details.a: Three. A majority is 4, so up to 3 can fail and the group still commits. General rule: N = 2f + 1 for f failures.

details.q: A team wants a 4-node group instead of 3 to be safer. What do they get?
details.a: Nothing for availability: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority and still tolerate one failure. They pay for an extra node and gain a worse tie risk (2/2 split leaves nobody a majority). Use 3 or 5.

details.q: A 5-node cluster splits into 3 and 2. What should happen?
details.a: The 3-node side keeps committing; the 2-node side must refuse writes (and linearizable reads). Clients reaching the minority see errors or timeouts rather than divergent data.

details.q: How do consensus quorums differ from Dynamo-style tunable quorums?
details.a: Consensus: an elected leader, a single ordered log, an entry is committed on a majority, strong consistency. Tunable: no leader, per-request W/R, concurrent writes possible, eventual convergence with repair.

Every commit waits for the node that completes the majority, so latency is set by the median-speed replica; across regions that is a cross-region round trip. Also 2f + 1 nodes of storage and no answers without a majority.

details.q: Do quorums protect against corrupted or malicious replicas?
details.a: No. They tolerate crash faults and network partitions. Byzantine faults need different protocols with more replicas.

prompts.q: Explain why majority quorums prevent split brain and what they cost.
points: Any two majorities overlap in a node
Two disjoint partitions cannot both commit
Cost: majority round trip per commit

prompts.q: Compare tunable quorums and consensus quorums and say when you pick each.
points: Tunable: leaderless, W + R > N, available, eventually consistent
Consensus: leader + log + majority commit, single history
Consensus for metadata, locks, config, leader election

prompts.q: Pick the cluster size for tolerating two failures and justify it.
points: Even sizes add cost with no extra tolerance
Place across failure domains so no domain holds a majority
